etymology: Latin Prisca, “ancient” or “venerable,” the formal name of Priscilla, wife of Aquila and fellow-labourer of Paul.
biblical_def: Prisca is the name Paul gives to Priscilla, the wife of Aquila, a tentmaker like himself, with whom he abode and wrought at Corinth (Act 18:2–3). Driven from Rome when Claudius commanded all Jews to depart, she and her husband came to be among the most beloved of Paul’s fellow-labourers in Christ Jesus. In the salutations of the sixteenth chapter of Romans, Paul writes, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus: who have for my life laid down their own necks” (Rom 16:3–4), naming a couple who had ventured their very lives for him. When the eloquent Apollos came to Ephesus mighty in the Scriptures, knowing only the baptism of John, Aquila and Priscilla took him unto them, and “expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26). It is worthy of note that this private instruction was given by a married couple together, in keeping with the order of God’s house, not by a woman teaching with authority in the assembly. Prisca stands as a witness that a godly wife, labouring in submission alongside her husband, may be a great helper in the gospel; that the communion of saints binds husband and wife in one service to Christ; and that the LORD remembers by name those who hazard their lives for His ministers.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the godly wife who labours in the Lord beside her husband. Prisca and Aquila are named together as helpers in Christ Jesus who laid down their own necks for Paul; theirs was a shared service, ordered and harmonious, the wife labouring in submission alongside her husband. She did not teach with authority in the assembly, but in the home, with her husband, expounded the way of God more perfectly to a gifted man who lacked light. So a godly wife may be a great helper in the gospel, edifying the church within the bounds the LORD has set.

etymology: Latin Amplias, a shortened form of Ampliatus, “enlarged” or “extended,” a believer at Rome whom Paul calls his beloved.
biblical_def: Amplias is named but once in all of Scripture, in the long roll of greetings that closes the epistle to the Romans: “Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord” (Rom 16:8). Nothing more is told of him; we know not his station, his labours, nor his end. Yet the few words that name him are weighty beyond measure, for the great apostle calls him “my beloved in the Lord.” His name, a common one borne often by servants and freedmen of the Roman household, suggests a man of humble or even servile rank; and it is striking that the gospel had so knit this obscure man to Paul that the apostle should send him a personal salutation across the sea. Here is the communion of saints in its sweetness: a bond of love in the Lord that crosses every barrier of rank and distance, and that the Holy Ghost saw fit to set down forever in the inspired record. Amplias stands as a witness that Christ knows His own by name, however unknown they may be to the world; that the least and lowliest of believers is precious to the saints and to the Saviour; and that to be “beloved in the Lord” is a higher honour than any the world can give. His name is written in Scripture, and, what is more, in the Lamb’s book of life.

etymology: Latin Urbanus, “of the city” or “courteous,” a fellow-worker at Rome whom Paul calls his helper in Christ.
biblical_def: Urbane, more properly Urbanus, is named once in Scripture, in the greetings that close the epistle to the Romans: “Salute Urbane, our helper in Christ, and Stachys my beloved” (Rom 16:9). The name, meaning “of the city,” was common among the freedmen of Rome, and may mark Urbane as a man of humble station who had been brought low in the world but raised high in Christ. Paul calls him not “my helper” but “our helper in Christ,” a fellow-labourer who served not Paul alone but the whole company of the saints and the cause of the gospel itself. The word translated “helper” bespeaks one who works together with others in a common labour; Urbane was such a man, a true yokefellow in the work of the Lord. Of his particular deeds nothing is recorded, yet the apostle’s testimony that he was a fellow-worker in Christ is honour enough. Urbane stands as a witness to the dignity of labour in the Lord: that the saints are knit together as fellow-workers in one great cause, and that the humblest servant who labours faithfully for the gospel is remembered by name in the eternal record, his work not forgotten before God, who is not unrighteous to forget the labour of love shown toward His name.

etymology: Greek Herodion, “heroic” or “belonging to Herod,” a believer at Rome whom Paul calls his kinsman.
biblical_def: Herodion is named once in Scripture, among the greetings that close the epistle to the Romans: “Salute Herodion my kinsman” (Rom 16:11). His name, which bears the mark of the house of Herod, suggests that he may have been a freedman or servant connected with that family, a Jew who had come to faith in the very Messiah whom the Herods had opposed and persecuted. Paul calls him “my kinsman,” a term he uses of several in this chapter, signifying most likely a fellow Israelite, one of Paul’s kinsmen according to the flesh, for whom the apostle bore a great and grieving love (Rom 9:3). Thus Herodion was twice bound to Paul: by the blood of Israel, and, far more deeply, by the blood of Christ that makes the saints one. Of his life and labours nothing else is told. Yet his place in the inspired record bears witness that the gospel had reached even into households once hostile to the Lord, and that grace had made a brother of one whose very name recalled the enemies of Christ. Herodion stands as a witness that the communion of saints is thicker than the ties of nature, binding kinsmen of the flesh together yet more closely in the household of faith; and that Christ gathers His own out of every house, even the houses of His foes.

etymology: Greek Narkissos, the name of a flower; a man of Rome whose household held believers in the Lord.
biblical_def: Narcissus is named once in Scripture, in the greetings of the sixteenth chapter of Romans: “Greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord” (Rom 16:11). It is worthy of careful note that Paul does not greet Narcissus himself, but only those of his household who are “in the Lord.” Narcissus was a wealthy Roman name, borne by a famous freedman of the emperor Claudius; whether this be the same man or another, the master of the house appears not to have been a believer. Yet within his household — among his servants, freedmen, and dependents — there were those who belonged to Christ, a little company of saints gathered under the roof of an unbelieving lord. Paul singles them out with tender care: not all the household, but “them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.” Here is a sweet and humbling picture of the early church: bondservants and lowly men, set in great households not their own, yet partakers of a liberty their masters knew not. Narcissus, or rather his household, stands as a witness that the grace of God springs up in the most unlikely soil; that the Lord has His own hidden in the houses of the great and the worldly; and that Christ knows each of His own by name, even the servant in an unbelieving master’s house.

etymology: Latin Rufus, “red” or “red-haired,” a believer at Rome chosen in the Lord, likely the son of Simon of Cyrene.
biblical_def: Rufus is named in the greetings of Romans: “Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine” (Rom 16:13). He is very likely the same Rufus named in the Gospel of Mark, where Simon of Cyrene, compelled to bear the cross of Christ, is called “the father of Alexander and Rufus” (Mar 15:21) — a notice that would have meaning only if his sons were known to the church for whom Mark wrote. If so, Rufus was the son of the man who carried the Saviour’s cross to Golgotha, and the blessing that fell upon that house through so solemn an errand is a marvel of providence. Paul calls him “chosen in the Lord,” a phrase that breathes the sovereign electing grace of God, for the saints are chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4). And with tender affection he greets the mother of Rufus as “his mother and mine,” testifying that this godly woman had shown Paul such motherly kindness that he counted her his own mother in the faith. Rufus stands as a witness to the riches of electing grace, that the Lord marks out His own; and to the sweetness of the communion of saints, in which a brother is chosen in the Lord and a sister becomes a mother to a stranger for Christ’s sake.

etymology: Greek Hermas, a shortened form of a name such as Hermagoras; a believer at Rome greeted by Paul.
biblical_def: Hermas is named once in Scripture, in the cluster of greetings that closes the epistle to the Romans: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Rom 16:14). He is one of a little band of saints greeted together, perhaps a household or a small assembly that met as a church among themselves. His name, a common one among the servant and freedman class of Rome, derived from the heathen god Hermes, marks him likely as a man of humble birth, perhaps once a bondservant, now a brother in Christ. Of his life nothing else is told; he must not be confused with the later second-century writer of the same name to whom the work called The Shepherd is ascribed, which is no part of inspired Scripture. The whole company — Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes — are passed over with a single greeting, named and then named no more. Yet that they are named at all, in the very Word of God, is honour beyond reckoning. Hermas stands as a witness that Christ knows His own by name, and forgets none of the lowliest of His servants; that the brethren who gather together in His name are precious to Him; and that obscurity before men is no obscurity before the Lord, who has written the names of His people in heaven.

etymology: Greek Aristoboulos, “best counsellor” or “best counselling,” a man of Rome whose household held believers.
biblical_def: Aristobulus is named once in Scripture, in the greetings of Romans: “Salute them which are of Aristobulus' household” (Rom 16:10). As with Narcissus a verse later, Paul does not greet the man himself, but those of his household who belonged to Christ. Aristobulus bore a princely Greek name, “best counsellor,” and some have thought him to be a grandson of Herod the Great, a man of rank dwelling at Rome; whether so or not, the master of the house seems not to have been a believer, while certain of his servants, freedmen, and dependents were saints of the Lord. Paul sends his greeting through them, a little flock gathered within a great worldly house. The careful wording — not “Aristobulus,” but “them which are of Aristobulus' household” — shows the apostle’s precision in distinguishing the true saints from the household at large. Aristobulus, or rather his household, stands as a witness that the gospel had taken root even in the homes of the noble and the heathen, gathering out a people for Christ from among bondservants and dependents; and that the Lord, who knows them that are His, has His own scattered in the most unlikely places, never forgetting the lowliest believer who serves an earthly master while owning a heavenly Lord.

etymology: Greek Sosipatros, “saviour of his father” or “deliverer,” a kinsman of Paul who joined in the greetings of Romans.
biblical_def: Sosipater is named in the closing chapter of Romans among those who sent their own greetings to the saints at Rome through Paul’s pen: “Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you” (Rom 16:21). Unlike most named in that chapter, who are greeted by Paul, Sosipater is one of those who, being with Paul as he wrote, joined in sending salutation. Paul calls him “my kinsman,” most likely meaning a fellow Israelite according to the flesh. He is very probably the same as Sopater of Berea, the son of Pyrrhus, who accompanied Paul into Asia (Act 20:4), Sopater being a shortened form of the longer Sosipater. If so, he was one of the trusted companions who travelled with the apostle in the work of the gospel, perhaps among those who bore the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem. His name, “saviour of his father,” though a common Greek name, may sweetly picture the believer who, by his faith and prayers, becomes a means of blessing to his house. Sosipater stands as a witness to the fellowship of labour in the Lord, in which kinsmen and companions are bound together in one great work; and to the quiet faithfulness of those who travel and toil unseen, their names preserved forever in the record of the saints.
webster_summary: A kinsman of Paul who joined in the greetings of Romans; likely the Sopater of Berea who travelled with Paul (Rom 16:21).

corruption_summary: A saint of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses to the fellowship of labour and the quiet faithfulness of Paul’s companions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fellowship of labour in the Lord, in which kinsmen and companions are bound together in one great work. Sosipater, with Timothy, Lucius, and Jason, joined in greeting the saints at Rome; they were Paul’s kinsmen and fellow-workers, knit to him by the blood of Israel and the bond of the gospel. The apostle did not labour alone, but in a company of faithful men who shared his toil.

If Sosipater be the Sopater of Berea who travelled with Paul into Asia, he also witnesses to the quiet faithfulness of those who toil unseen. Such men accompanied the apostle on hard journeys, bore the gifts of the churches, and shared his perils, yet are named but once or twice in passing. Their service was great though their fame was small; and the LORD, who forgets no labour of love, has preserved their names forever in the record of His saints.

etymology: Latin Crescens, “growing” or “increasing,” a companion of Paul who departed unto Galatia in the work of the gospel.
biblical_def: Crescens is named once in Scripture, in the last epistle Paul wrote, as the apostle, awaiting his death at Rome, told Timothy of those who had gone from him: “For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia” (2Ti 4:10). Care must be taken here, for the verse names Demas, who forsook the apostle out of love for the world, in the same breath with Crescens and Titus, who departed otherwise. There is no warrant to charge Crescens with the apostasy of Demas. The natural reading is that Demas alone forsook Paul, while Crescens and Titus were sent or went forth in the service of the gospel — Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia — even as Paul elsewhere dispatched his fellow-labourers to the churches. So Crescens was most likely a faithful companion, gone on a true errand of ministry while the apostle was left in his chains with Luke alone. His name, “growing” or “increasing,” fits a labourer sent that the gospel might grow and increase in the regions beyond. Crescens stands as a witness to the labour of the unknown servants of Christ, who go where they are sent and are named but once; and to the costly fellowship of the gospel, in which workers must part from one another for the sake of the churches.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the labour of the unknown servant sent in the work of the gospel. Care must be taken not to over-read the verse: though Crescens is named in the same breath as Demas, who forsook Paul for love of the world, the natural reading is that Demas alone forsook him, while Crescens and Titus went forth in ministry. Crescens departed to Galatia as a faithful labourer, gone where the gospel must grow and increase.

Crescens also witnesses to the costly fellowship of the gospel, in which workers must often part from one another for the sake of the churches. While the aged apostle sat in his chains with Luke alone beside him, Crescens was away in Galatia and Titus in Dalmatia, scattered abroad in service. Such partings are no failure of love but the price of the work; and the LORD remembers by name the servant who goes quietly where he is sent, though Scripture tell us nothing more of him.
